explanations: luna: The section connects water with the growth that feeds living things; this verse says rain brings fruits as provision on the earth made as a dwelling place. | terra: God sends water from the sky and brings out fruits as provision, so the food a person might withhold is first identified as divine supply.

luna: Against the section’s blocked watercourse, God brings twelve springs from the rock and tells the tribes to eat and drink from His provision (كُلُوا وَاشْرَبُوا مِن رِّزْقِ اللَّهِ). | terra: God makes twelve springs burst from the rock, each people knows its drinking place, and all are told to eat and drink from God's provision; flowing water is apportioned for communal access rather than blocked.

luna: The source explicitly names the root m-n-ʿ for preventing good and pictures a blocked watercourse; this verse uses the same root for barring people from God’s mosques, extending that act of obstructing access to a shared good.
terra: Abraham asks that the town be secure and that its people receive fruits, joining a stable place to supplied food in the same relation as the section's watered shelter.
terra: Rain revives the earth after death and living creatures are dispersed through it; this supplies both the watered ground and the animal life sustained by its growth.

terra: The fasting compensation of طَعَامُ مِسْكِينٍ uses the section's two named words for a concrete due owed to a poor person; the section's dictionary extension asks the reader to hear drink within that subsistence.

luna: The source explicitly extends the dictionary form ṭaʿām to water; in Ṭālūt’s river test, whoever does not yaṭʿamhu (taste/drink it) is not of his company, so the verse makes that extension concrete. | terra: The section explicitly uses وَمَن لَمْ يَطْعَمْهُ of Talut's river to show that طعم can make water an object of tasting, so "feeding" the poor reaches the provision of drink.

terra: Showy spending is soil on rock stripped bare by a downpour; water produces no lasting benefit where giving is performance, a pointed reversal of the section's water that enters earth and sustains others.

terra: Sincere spending is pictured as a garden on a رَبْوَة struck by rain and yielding double produce; water, high ground, fruit, and generous release form the positive counterpart to the withholding hand.
terra: Believers are told to spend from good earnings and from what God brings out of the earth, carrying water-grown produce onward as human giving.
terra: Those who hoard what God gave from His bounty mistake the withholding for good; the ayah reinforces the section's distinction between receiving provision and owning its source.

luna: The source says a person withholds water that was not made by his hand; this verse condemns miserliness, urging others to be miserly, and concealing God’s bounty, a specific parallel in how received provision is kept back. | terra: The miserly both urge miserliness and conceal what God gave them from His bounty, closely matching the section's person who treats a received flow as something to stop.

terra: Against the charge that God's hand is fettered, the ayah says His hands are outspread and He gives as He wills; open divine giving supplies the direct contrary to the section's closed, withholding hand.
terra: Feeding ten poor people as expiation makes the section's named food and poor recipients a concrete, measured obligation rather than optional surplus.

luna: The section traces water into growth on the ground; this verse repeats that sequence as water from the sky brings out varied plants, grain, and fruit. | terra: Water from heaven brings forth the growth of all things, including green growth, grain, and fruit; it elaborates what the section compresses into earth drinking and pasture emerging.

luna: The section condemns failing to urge food for the poor; this verse tells people to eat the crop’s fruit and give its due on harvest day, a concrete rule for sharing field produce. | terra: After naming productive gardens and crops, the ayah commands giving their due at harvest; it carries water-grown abundance into an enforceable human share, the opposite of arresting its benefit at one's hand.

luna: The section’s water reaches ground and enables growth; here a heavy cloud is driven to dead land, rain is sent, and fruit is brought forth, a specific rain-to-yield scene. | terra: Heavy clouds are driven to dead land, water descends, and fruits come forth; the ayah presents the same directed movement from source to receptive earth and produce.
terra: Good land yields vegetation by its Lord's leave, whereas bad land yields only scant growth; the contrast shows that receiving the same water is not identical with passing on its benefit.

luna: This retelling likewise gives the tribes twelve springs from a rock and tells them to eat and drink from God’s provision; it repeats the shared-water scene that contrasts with withholding. | terra: The parallel Moses scene makes twelve springs issue, assigns each community its drinking place, and couples water with God's food provision, concretely linking water, settlement, and shared sustenance.

luna: The section pictures a hand stopping water and withholding help; this verse describes hypocrites as physically withholding their hands and forbidding good, a specific parallel in the act of keeping aid back. | terra: The hypocrites "close their hands," giving the section's withholding hand an exact ethical gesture and showing refusal to let received good pass onward.

luna: The source says the water-holder did not originate the supply; this verse describes rain-grown vegetation, then a land whose owners think they control it before it is cut down, exposing that claim’s limit. | terra: Rain mingles with the earth's vegetation from which people and cattle eat, closely matching the section's chain from descending water to shared pasture and food.
terra: The Children of Israel are lodged in a sound settlement and provided good things, pairing dwelling with supplied sustenance as the section pairs قرار with water.

terra: The earth is commanded to swallow its water, the sky to stop, and the flood subsides; this divine closing of the water's course marks the boundary between providential control and a human's blameworthy obstruction.
terra: The brothers say مُنِعَ مِنَّا ٱلْكَيْلُ, that their food measure will be withheld; the same root is thus used for stopping essential provision, clarifying the force of withholding al-māʿūn.

luna: The source names the channels of water in a valley; here water runs through valleys (فَسَالَتْ أَوْدِيَةٌ بِقَدَرِهَا), and the verse’s foam-versus-benefit parable makes the useful flow distinct from what passes. | terra: Water runs through valley channels, each according to its measure, and the flood carries foam while what benefits people remains; this realizes both the section's watercourse and its useful gift.

luna: This verse joins water sent from the sky, fruit provided to people, and rivers made serviceable; it gives another concrete scene of water and provision that matches the section’s flow-to-growth path. | terra: Rain produces fruits as provision and rivers are subjected for people, bringing the source, edible result, and ongoing watercourse into one divine gift.

terra: Abraham settles his descendants in an uncultivated valley and asks that they receive fruits; unlike the naturally watered pasture of the section, their staying depends visibly on God's provision and human gratitude.
terra: God sends water, gives it to people to drink, and says they are not its keepers; that directly sharpens the section's charge against a hand that blocks water it did not originate or possess.
terra: Livestock are beautiful when brought home and when sent out to pasture, a concrete picture of the herd's movement between its settled place and grazing ground.

luna: Rain is drink and brings forth vegetation where livestock graze (فِيهِ تُسِيمُونَ); this directly joins water to pasture, as the section’s explanation of how water feeds the ground and keeps animals there does. | terra: Water from heaven becomes both human drink and vegetation in which livestock graze, exactly joining flowing provision to the pasture that lets a herd remain.

luna: This verse says the water produces crops and fruit; 16:10 names the same rain, drink, and grazing vegetation, completing the section’s route from water to growth and provision. | terra: The water of 16:10 grows crops, olives, palms, grapes, and every fruit; it develops the human-food side of the same water that creates pasture.

luna: The source’s dictionary gloss for miskin describes a pasture so ample there is no need to leave for ظعن; this verse names dwellings and animal-fiber goods usable on a day of travel or a day of staying, giving that movement/staying contrast a concrete scene. | terra: Homes are made سَكَنًا, while livestock hides make dwellings useful on the day of ظَعْن and the day of staying; this exactly unfolds the section's dictionary contrast between settled pasture and departure.
terra: Following the dwellings of 16:80, God provides shade and mountain shelters; it continues the concrete account of what makes a place habitable and protective.

luna: The source’s dictionary gloss for miskin connects staying to abundance; this verse describes a secure, tranquil town receiving provision abundantly, then losing that ease to hunger after denying God’s favors, a specific reversal of settled provision. | terra: A town secure and at ease receives abundant provision from every place, then ingratitude turns that condition into hunger and fear; settlement and food are thus joined, with their loss marking the boundary.
terra: God extends His gift to both groups and His gift is not restricted; the unrestricted divine giving forms a thematic boundary against a human hand that arrests benefit.
terra: The command not to keep one's hand chained to one's neck gives the withholding disposition a bodily image closely matching the hand that blocks the section's channel.

luna: The source follows water into productive ground; this garden scene says both gardens yielded their fruit and a river was made to flow between them (وَفَجَّرْنَا خِلَالَهُمَا نَهَرًا), joining water and yield. | terra: A river is made to gush between two fruitful gardens, joining a watercourse through land to sustained produce.

luna: The section’s flowing supply can be obstructed, yet was not produced by the person who withholds it; the garden owner’s water becomes غَوْرًا and cannot be reached, a direct boundary on human control. | terra: A garden's water may become غَوْرًا and impossible to retrieve; this is the explicit reverse of accessible flowing مَعِين and illuminates what is at stake when 67:30 asks who can restore it.

luna: The section’s dictionary pasture is abundant enough to keep animals in place; this verse’s water-grown vegetation becomes scattered dry debris, a specific reversal of that lush field image. | terra: Water from heaven mingles with earth's vegetation before it becomes dry fragments; the ayah traces the same water-to-growth process while exposing its temporal limit.
terra: In the other Qur'anic scene of Mary, she is told not to grieve because God has placed a سَرِيّ beneath her, commonly understood here as a stream; it supplies water at her place of refuge.
terra: Mary is told to shake the palm so fresh dates fall to her; between the stream in 19:24 and eating and drinking in 19:26, the act shows supplied shelter becoming food in hand.
terra: Mary is told to eat, drink, and be comforted after the stream and dates are provided, joining shelter to the two forms of sustenance that the section holds together.

luna: The verse puts earth’s paths, rainwater, and varied plants in one scene; the source’s waterbeds in valleys and the water that makes pasture grow meet this same route through land. | terra: God sends water and brings forth diverse plants from it; this supplies the section's movement from water through earth to vegetation.

luna: The source describes pasture that lets animals remain; this verse says to eat and graze livestock (كُلُوا وَارْعَوْا أَنْعَامَكُمْ), following 20:53’s rain and plant growth. | terra: "Eat and pasture your livestock" states the two beneficiaries of the plants in 20:53, matching the section's food and abundant grazing ground.
terra: Life in the Garden is defined by neither hunger nor nakedness, setting a boundary in which settled shelter includes reliable food and covering.
terra: The Garden also excludes thirst and exposure to the sun, completing the link between habitation, drink, and protection that the section finds in a well-watered refuge.
terra: Every living thing is made from water, grounding the section's more specific chain from water to grass, herd, and human food in water's general life-giving role.
luna: The section says water reaches soil and makes pasture grow; this verse describes land swelling and producing every kind of lovely growth after rain.
terra: Ruined settlements are pictured beside an abandoned well; the conjunction of a lost water source and emptied habitation reverses the section's flowing water that enables staying.
terra: "Have you not seen" rain descend and the earth become green; the stance of seeing and the ground's response both echo the section's directed question about water.

luna: The source says the water is not something the blocker made; here God sends it in measure, settles it in the earth (فَأَسْكَنَّاهُ), and can take it away, making control of the supply the boundary. | terra: Measured water descends and is made to lodge in the earth, while God can take it away; the ayah supplies the section's descent, saturation, settlement, and dependence on the true giver.

luna: The source’s maʿīn is flowing water; this verse joins it to qarār, a settled place, in God’s shelter for Mary and her son, matching the section’s water-bearing refuge and abundant pasture where animals can stay. | terra: This is the section's explicit shelter scene: Mary and her son are lodged on a رَبْوَةٍ ذَاتِ قَرَارٍ وَمَعِينٍ, joining a place fit for settled life to flowing water.
terra: People of bounty are told not to swear off giving relatives, the poor, and emigrants; the ayah directly reverses an attempted blockage of benefit by a hand that has itself received bounty.
terra: A thirsty person takes a mirage for water but finds none on arrival; inaccessible, illusory water is a precise reversal of the available مَعِين developed by the section.

luna: The source treats water as provision that reaches the land; this verse calls the sent-down water pure, and 25:49 completes the scene with dead land revived and livestock watered. | terra: Pure water is sent from heaven; 25:49 then states its effects on dead land, animals, and people, so this row contributes the source and quality of the flow.

luna: The source describes water nourishing land and pasture; this verse says the water revives a dead town and waters livestock and people, while 25:48 names the water sent down. | terra: Pure rain revives dead country and gives drink to many humans and cattle; it joins restored land, watering, and herd provision as the section does.
terra: The water has been distributed among people so that they remember, yet most respond with ingratitude; distribution and refusal add a moral frame to the provision described in 25:48-49.
terra: Abraham identifies God as the one who feeds him and gives him drink, joining the section's two forms of sustenance at their true source.
terra: The people are asked whether they expect to remain secure among gardens and springs, directly linking settled security to abundant water.
terra: Crops and palms complete the gardens-and-springs setting of 26:147, showing the edible growth that makes such staying possible.

luna: The source depicts water being kept back from others; here the she-camel and the people each have an allotted drinking day (لَهَا شِرْبٌ وَلَكُمْ شِرْبُ يَوْمٍ مَّعْلُومٍ), a specific counter-scene of shared water. | terra: The she-camel has a drinking share and the people a share on a known day, another concrete boundary governing access to the common water on which herds and humans depend.

luna: The source’s central claim is that a person holds back water they did not originate; here God sends water that grows beautiful gardens and asks who else could do this. | terra: The rhetorical question asks who sent water down and grew splendid gardens that humans could not grow, directing attention from the result to the giver just as the section does.

luna: The section names valley watercourses; this verse asks who placed rivers through the earth and set barriers between bodies of water, continuing the creation-and-water scene of 27:60. | terra: God makes the earth a place of settlement, قَرَارًا, and places rivers through it; this is a close nonlexical twin to the section's pairing of stable habitation and مَعِين.

luna: The section links a water source to animals and their sustenance; at Midian’s watering place, shepherds water their flocks while two women wait back, making access to water for herds the scene. | terra: At Midian, people water their flocks while two women hold theirs back until the shepherds leave; access to water, herd movement, and an obstructed turn at the source meet in one concrete scene.

luna: The section’s figure impedes a resource; Moses instead draws water for the two women’s flock (فَسَقَىٰ لَهُمَا), a specific act of supplying water to people waiting at the well. | terra: Moses waters the women's flock for them, reversing the blocked access of 28:23 and embodying the section's opposite of the hand that withholds a life-sustaining flow.
terra: A secure sanctuary receives fruits gathered from every kind as provision from God, linking stable habitation to food brought into it.

terra: Towns exulting in their livelihood become dwellings scarcely inhabited afterward; lost provision and lost settlement together reverse the section's nourishing water that permits continued residence.
terra: Asked who sends water from heaven and revives dead earth, the addressees must answer "God"; this is a direct parallel to the section's question about who brings flowing water.
terra: Water descends from the sky and revives the earth after death, repeating the causal movement on which the section's pasture scene depends.
terra: Water sent from heaven causes every noble kind of growth, supplying the vegetation stage of the section's watercourse.

luna: Water is driven to barren land, crops are brought out for people and their livestock; this directly stages the section’s water-to-soil-to-animal provision. | terra: The question "do they not see" points to water driven into barren land, crops brought out, and both livestock and people eating, reproducing the section's whole water-to-food chain.

terra: Whatever mercy God opens none can withhold, and whatever He withholds none can release; this establishes the theological boundary behind the section's human attempt to dam a gift whose source he does not control.

luna: The section connects water to food-bearing ground; this verse describes dead earth made alive and grain brought out for people to eat, while 36:34 continues with gardens and springs. | terra: The dead earth is revived and grain brought from it for people to eat; 36:34 supplies the gardens and springs that make this food-chain connection explicit.

luna: This verse joins gardens to springs made to gush forth (وَفَجَّرْنَا فِيهَا مِنَ الْعُيُونِ), a direct image of water flowing into productive ground; 36:33 names the grain from that land. | terra: Gardens are supplied by springs made to gush within them, a direct scene of water coursing through productive ground.

luna: The section extends feeding to water; this verse turns the preceding garden-and-spring scene into fruit for eating, following 36:34’s springs and gardens. | terra: People eat the resulting fruit and are asked for gratitude in relation to what their hands did not produce; this supports the section's insistence that the withholder did not make the flow.

terra: Those told to spend from God's provision refuse by asking why they should feed someone God could feed; the ayah exposes exactly the false inference the image rejects—divine provision does not excuse a human block in its passage.

luna: The source glosses maʿīn as flowing water; this paradise scene serves a cup from maʿīn (كَأْسٍ مِّن مَّعِينٍ), using the named word in another setting. | terra: A cup from مَعِين is passed around in the Garden; it preserves the section's dictionary sense of accessible flowing water while showing it freely circulated as drink.
terra: Job is given a cool spring for washing and drinking, showing accessible water as God's restorative provision for both body and thirst.

luna: The section says flowing water reaches soil and grows pasture; this verse describes water channeled as springs through earth and crops, then those crops yellow and become debris, setting growth beside its loss. | terra: "Have you not seen" introduces rain conducted as springs through the earth and then varied crops; it directly supplies the hidden channels and watered growth behind the section's image.

luna: The section describes water reaching soil and producing growth; this verse says earth that looks lifeless stirs and swells when water is sent down, and attributes that revival to God. | terra: Water makes the humbled earth stir and swell, another direct formulation of ground receiving water and becoming productive.
luna: This verse names paths made through the earth (سُبُلًا); 43:11 continues with water sent down in measure and land revived, recalling the section’s watercourses through valleys.

luna: This verse describes measured rain reviving a dead town; 43:10 immediately before it names the paths through the earth, together giving a specific land-and-water scene parallel to the section’s channels. | terra: Water descends in measure and revives dead land, joining measured supply to receptive earth in the same causal relation as the section.
terra: The promised Garden contains rivers of water that does not spoil, presenting an enduring, unobstructed flow as the positive boundary to water that sinks or is withheld.
terra: Whoever is miserly is miserly only against himself, while God is rich and humans are needy; the ayah exposes the dependence of the person who tries to arrest a received benefit.

luna: The section follows water into pasture and provision; this verse describes blessed rain producing gardens and grain, another specific water-to-crop scene. | terra: Blessed water grows gardens and harvested grain, directly joining received water to food that can pass to people.

luna: This verse calls the preceding rain-grown yield provision for servants and says it revives dead land; 50:9 supplies the water, gardens, and grain at the start of the passage. | terra: The growth in 50:9-10 is provision for servants and revival of dead land, naming both recipient and effect of the watered earth.
terra: مَنَّاعٍ لِّلْخَيْرِ is the very dictionary wording invoked by the section, identifying habitual obstruction of good as the human character behind blocking the channel.
terra: A recognized right belongs in their wealth to the asker and deprived, making the received good a channel with a due outlet rather than unrestricted private control.
luna: This verse introduces the she-camel as the test for Salih’s people; 54:28 then gives the specific water-sharing arrangement between them and the camel.

luna: The section shows a person blocking a watercourse; in Salih’s people’s test, water is explicitly a share between them (الْمَاءُ قِسْمَةٌ بَيْنَهُمْ), with a turn for each drinker. | terra: The water is declared a share divided among the people and the she-camel, with each turn attended; this makes access to water a divinely set right rather than a benefit one party may obstruct.
luna: After 54:28 assigns shares of water, this verse says the people called their companion, who hamstrung the she-camel, completing the passage’s reversal of the shared-water arrangement.
terra: Two springs flow in the two gardens; عَيْنَانِ تَجْرِيَانِ provides a direct nonlexical formulation of the running-water scene.
terra: Two gushing springs offer a more forceful form of accessible water, extending the section's concern with an unobstructed source.

luna: The source glosses maʿīn as flowing water; this paradise passage also names cups from maʿīn (كَأْسٍ مِّن مَّعِينٍ), carrying the word into a different drinking scene. | terra: Cups, ewers, and a cup from مَعِين present flowing water in vessels and in circulation, a direct lexical development of the section's final word as water rather than merely an object of aid.
terra: Garden fruit is neither cut off nor مَمْنُوعَةٍ; unwithheld abundance gives the lexical and material opposite of the hand that prevents a small necessary benefit.

luna: The section traces water to pasture growth; this adjacent passage asks what people cultivate, then 56:64 asks who actually makes it grow, before 56:68 turns to drinking water. | terra: "Have you seen what you sow?" extends the same seeing-question used for water in 56:68 to the crop produced after water enters the earth.

luna: The source says the withholding person did not make the water; this verse asks whether people or God make the crop grow, just before 56:68–69 asks who sends down drinking water. | terra: The question whether humans make the sowing grow or God does prevents the recipient from claiming authorship of the pasture or food that later passes through human hands.
luna: The section describes the pasture’s life-giving growth; this verse says God could turn the crop to dry debris, and the following 56:68–70 makes water’s source and vulnerability explicit.

luna: The section says the Quran turns an “Have you seen?” question toward water; this verse asks whether the hearers have considered the water they drink, and 56:69 names its divine source. | terra: أَفَرَءَيْتُمُ ٱلْمَاءَ ٱلَّذِى تَشْرَبُونَ directs the "have you seen" stance toward drinking water, as the section says the opening question should be directed toward its final water image.

luna: The source insists the flowing water does not originate in the withholding hand; this verse asks whether people sent drinking water down from the clouds or God did (أَأَنْتُمْ أَنْزَلْتُمُوهُ مِنَ الْمُزْنِ أَمْ نَحْنُ الْمُنْزِلُونَ). | terra: The question whether people sent the water down or God did identifies the source of the flow and exposes the absurdity of treating it as the withholder's own.

luna: The section’s hand can block a watercourse but cannot determine its source; this continuation says God could make drinking water bitter (أُجَاجًا), showing a further limit on human control. | terra: God could make the drinking water bitter; this boundary to 56:68-69 shows that drinkability itself is given, deepening the blame of withholding usable water without gratitude.

luna: This is an interpretive extension of the section’s abundant pasture image: here rain-grown vegetation first pleases its cultivators, then yellows and becomes debris, showing how such growth can pass.
luna: This verse repeats the pattern of miserliness and hiding what God has bestowed; it matches the section’s claim that the withheld water is not the withholder’s creation.
terra: Feeding sixty poor people is required when the other expiation is impossible, another legal setting in which sustenance must reach the poor.

luna: The section connects ample pasture with no need to migrate away; here hypocrites explicitly urge that spending stop until the people around the Messenger disperse (لَا تُنفِقُوا عَلَىٰ مَنْ عِندَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ حَتَّىٰ يَنفَضُّوا), a specific reversal in which provision is withheld to force departure. | terra: The hypocrites propose stopping expenditure on the Prophet's companions until they disperse, while God's are the treasuries of heaven and earth; withheld provision here is explicitly intended to force departure, the reverse of abundant pasture permitting a group to stay.
terra: The command to lodge vulnerable women where the addressees dwell makes سكن an obligation to extend shelter, complementing the section's link between settlement and care.

terra: In the same surah as 67:30, the question asks who could provide if God withheld His provision; it distinguishes God's decisive control of supply from a human's blameworthy refusal to pass it on.

luna: The source glosses maʿīn as flowing water and says the surah’s opening question turns toward it; here the Prophet is told to ask who could restore water if it sinks away, locating the stream beyond the blocker’s control. | terra: This is the section's explicit convergence: the command "say, have you seen" turns the opening stance of surah 107 toward water, and مَاءٍ مَعِينٍ names the flowing water whose giver no human hand can replace.

luna: The source quotes the root form مَنَّاعٌ لِلْخَيْرِ for one who keeps goodness back; this ayah uses that same wording for a character who hinders good. | terra: The repeated description مَنَّاعٍ لِّلْخَيْرِ supplies the same habitual-withholder sense cited in the section and makes the withheld small benefit part of a settled moral type.

luna: The source’s failure is not urging food for the miskin; these garden owners deliberately plan that no poor person enter before the harvest (أَن لَّا يَدْخُلَنَّهَا الْيَوْمَ عَلَيْكُم مِّسْكِينٌ), a direct denial of provision. | terra: The garden owners conspire that no poor person shall enter upon them that day; their attempt to stop produce before it reaches the poor is the agricultural form of the section's blocked channel.

luna: This repeats the source’s wording from 107:3, «ولا يحض على طعام المسكين»; 69:33 gives the surrounding claim about not believing in God, so this row isolates the same failure to urge food for the poor. | terra: The condemned person does not urge طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ, the same formulation as 107:3; beside this section it makes withholding drink part of the same failure to sustain the poor.
terra: When good touches the anxious human he is مَنُوعًا, a withholding form from the same root; the ayah locates the blocked flow in the possessor's response to received good.
terra: Immediately after the portrait of the human as withholding in 70:21, the people of prayer have a known right in their wealth, offering the section's positive alternative.
terra: That known right is for the asker and deprived, identifying the outlet through which received good must move.
terra: Steadfastness is answered with abundant water, making plentiful water a supplied condition of flourishing rather than a human possession.
terra: The abundant water of 72:16 is also a test; that qualification parallels the river test in 2:249 and turns received provision into a measure of conduct.
terra: The people of the Fire confess that they did not feed the poor; this states as an omitted act what the section expands from food into water and settled subsistence.

luna: The source’s stream is a resource someone can block; here God’s servants drink from a spring that they make gush forth (عَيْنًا يَشْرَبُ بِهَا عِبَادُ اللَّهِ), followed in 76:8 by feeding the needy. | terra: God's servants drink from a spring and cause it to gush abundantly, presenting water as a gift whose course is opened and shared.

luna: Where the source’s figure withholds water and does not urge food for the needy, this passage feeds food to a poor person, an orphan, and a captive; 76:6 has just pictured a spring for God’s servants. | terra: The righteous give food they value to the poor, orphan, and captive; the food visibly passes through their hands instead of stopping there.

luna: The source’s withholding hand does not own the water it blocks; after the feeding scene in 76:8, this verse says the givers seek only God’s countenance and no reward or thanks, completing the opposing motive.
terra: Lofty mountains and fresh water given to drink bring height and potable water together, closely paralleling the high, well-watered refuge of 23:50.
terra: Abundant pouring water descends from rain clouds, supplying the first stage of the section's downward-moving flow.
terra: Grain and vegetation are brought out by that water, giving the next stage of the section's water-to-food movement.
terra: Dense gardens complete the result of the poured water in 78:14, a settled landscape made productive by the flow.

luna: The source’s secondary gloss for miskin invokes pasture, and 79:31 names both water and pasture (مَاءَهَا وَمَرْعَاهَا) as what is brought from the earth. | terra: God brings the earth's water and its pasture out of it, placing the two successive terms of the section's process in a single ayah.

luna: The source traces water into pasture for animals; this verse calls the preceding provision enjoyment for people and livestock (لَكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ), continuing 79:31’s water and pasture across 79:32. | terra: The water and pasture of 79:31 are provision for people and their livestock, confirming why a well-watered grazing place permits settled life.
terra: The command that the human being look at his food begins a scene that traces food backward to poured water, just as the section hears water inside طَعَام.

luna: The source traces water into pasture and provision; this passage starts by describing rain poured down (صَبَبْنَا الْمَاءَ صَبًّا), then names fruit and fodder at 80:31 and recipients at 80:32. | terra: The water is poured abundantly as the first material cause of the food named in 80:24; this makes explicit the section's claim that feeding reaches water.
terra: The earth is split after the water is poured, giving the section's saturated ground the opening through which its provision grows.
terra: Grain is the first named crop from the watered and split earth, making the food in 80:24 a concrete result rather than an isolated commodity.
terra: Grapes and fodder continue the water-grown sequence and bring human produce beside animal feed.
terra: Olives and palms extend the produce issuing from the watered earth and destined for use.
terra: Thick gardens form the productive habitat between poured water and the fruit and pasture of 80:31.

luna: The source’s water grows pasture; this verse names fruit and fodder (فَاكِهَةً وَأَبًّا), with 80:25 giving the rain at the start and 80:32 naming people and livestock as recipients. | terra: Fruit and pasture are named together in the water-grown sequence, joining human food to the grazing ground central to the section's account of settled animals.

luna: The source describes pasture sustaining animals; this verse says the preceding food and fodder are provision for people and livestock (لَكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ), continuing the rain-and-growth scene begun at 80:25. | terra: The sequence is declared provision for "you and your livestock," completing the same shared water-food-pasture economy developed by the section.

luna: The source’s secondary gloss develops pasture; this verse names pasture itself (الْمَرْعَىٰ) as what God brings forth, a direct verbal and field-image match. | terra: God brings out the pasture; although water is unstated here, the ayah isolates the grazing ground that the section treats as the outcome of water and the cause of a herd's staying.

luna: The source describes pasture as plentiful enough for animals to stay; this neighboring verse turns the pasture of 87:4 into dark debris (غُثَاءً أَحْوَىٰ), giving the growth a specific reversal.
terra: The people of the Fire drink from a boiling spring, reversing the beneficial flowing spring of 88:12 and showing that the mere presence of flowing drink does not make it merciful provision.
terra: A flowing spring, عَيْنٌ جَارِيَةٌ, states without the root م ع ن the exact dictionary gloss the section gives for مَعِين.

luna: This says people do not urge one another to feed the poor (وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ), extending the same negative feeding scene from 107:3 to a communal relation. | terra: وَلَا تَحَٰٓضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ nearly repeats 107:3 in the plural, confirming that failure even to urge the poor person's feeding is the social stoppage the water image exposes.

luna: The source’s 107:3 image is food urged for the poor; this verse names feeding on a day of hunger (إِطْعَامٌ فِي يَوْمٍ ذِي مَسْغَبَةٍ) as one concrete response to deprivation. | terra: Feeding on a day of hunger presents food as the released benefit in precisely the condition where withholding it is most consequential.
terra: The first recipient of that feeding is an orphan relative, linking sustenance to the vulnerable person whom 93:6 says God sheltered.

luna: The source names the miskin who is not urged food; this passage specifies a needy person in dust (مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ) as a recipient, while 90:14 names feeding during hunger. | terra: The other recipient is a poor person in misery, completing a concrete alternative to refusing طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ.
terra: The one who is miserly and considers himself self-sufficient embodies the inward claim behind blocking a provision whose source remains God.

luna: The source explicitly says the sheltering verb in 23:50 is the same as the orphan’s shelter here (فَآوَىٰ); this brings the section’s water-bearing refuge into relation to God’s shelter of a vulnerable child. | terra: The section explicitly links فَآوَىٰ to the shelter of 23:50: God finds an orphan and gives him refuge, establishing divine shelter as the model behind care for the vulnerable.
terra: Feeding against hunger and granting security against fear place subsistence and settled safety together, an indirect parallel to food, water, and refuge in the section.
